title: The localizing closure exists
statement:
Let $\Lambda$ be a condensed ring (not necessarily commutative) [sk-def-sfb-ring-object], $X$ a scheme with its small pro-étale site [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site], and $\Lambda_X=p_X^*\Lambda$ its pulled-back ring object [sk-def-sfb-pulled-back-coefficients]. Write $\mathcal A=\Mod_{\Lambda_X}$ for its category of left module objects [sk-def-sfb-module-objects], and $D(X_{\mathrm{proét}},\Lambda)=D(\mathcal A)$ for its unbounded derived category [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. All small sums and site skeletons use the fixed universe convention [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $\mathcal S$ be any class of objects of this derived category (for instance, when $\Lambda$ is commutative, $\mathcal S=\Dctf(X,\Lambda)$ of [det-def-sfb-constructible-tor-amplitude]).

1. $D(X_{\mathrm{proét}},\Lambda)$ has arbitrary small direct sums, computed termwise on complexes, and the direct sum of distinguished triangles is distinguished [def-weil-triangulated-category].
2. The intersection of all full triangulated subcategories of $D(X_{\mathrm{proét}},\Lambda)$ that contain $\mathcal S$, are closed under isomorphisms, and are closed under arbitrary small direct sums, is again such a subcategory. It is denoted $\Loc(\mathcal S)$; it is the smallest localizing subcategory containing $\mathcal S$. Here localizing means full, triangulated, closed under isomorphisms and under these sums.
3. $\Loc(\mathcal S)$ is closed under direct summands, hence thick [pur9-def-thick]; and $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal S'\subseteq\Loc(\mathcal S)$ implies $\Loc(\mathcal S')=\Loc(\mathcal S)$.

external.place: By exactness of direct sums, the acyclic complexes form a localizing subcategory of $K(\Lambda_X)$; for a Verdier quotient by a subcategory closed under coproducts, the quotient functor preserves coproducts (Neeman, *Triangulated categories*, Lemma 3.2.10).

proof.text: Identify the coefficient category with ordinary module sheaves, without assuming commutativity. For a ring object $R=\Lambda_X$ in tensor abelian sheaves, define on every object $U$ the operations $rs=\mu_U(r\otimes s)$ and $1_U=\eta_U(1)$. The ring-object axioms evaluated on pure tensors give associative unital rings $R(U)$; restrictions preserve these operations. For an internal module $(M,\gamma)$ put $rm=\gamma_U(r\otimes m)$. Conversely a sectionwise left action is a natural family of $\mathbf Z$-bilinear maps $R(U)\times M(U)\to M(U)$, so it extends uniquely to $R\otimes M\to M$ by [lem-pc-sites-sheaf-tensor-bilinear-universal], specialized to the constant ring sheaf $\mathbf Z$. An abelian sheaf is canonically a module over this sheaf: locally a section of $\mathbf Z$ is an integer, acting by repeated addition. Naturality and additivity imply linearity in those locally constant integers by checking on that cover. Consequently this tensor is the sheafified objectwise $\otimes_{\mathbf Z}$ used here, by the same bilinear universal property. Evaluating on pure tensors shows that the module axioms in the two descriptions agree. The two constructions are inverse, also on morphisms (the equation $f\gamma=\gamma'(R\otimes f)$ is exactly sectionwise linearity), giving an identification with the category of sheaves of left modules [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category] over the reconstructed ring sheaf. This is just the action definition [sk-def-sfb-module-objects] and the tensor definition [sk-def-sfb-sheaf-tensor]; no commutative-ring-module equivalence is used.

source.place: Tag 03CV, definition-sheaf-modules; elementary unpacking of internal actions using the sheaf tensor universal property

proof.text: Choose the small site skeleton and the coefficient universe as in [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site, def-weil-size-convention]. The ring-sheaf Grothendieck theorem [lem-weil-pbc-ring-sheaves-grothendieck] applies to this site and the ring sheaf reconstructed in step 1, including when $\Lambda$ is noncommutative. Thus $\mathcal A$ is Grothendieck abelian. Apply [lem-kun-grothendieck-derived-coproducts] to $\mathcal A$: for every small family of complexes $(K_i)$ its termwise coproduct represents the coproduct of $QK_i$ in $D(\mathcal A)$. Every derived object is represented by a complex by [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], so these give all the required direct sums, including the empty sum. This proves the existence and termwise assertion of (1).

source.place: Tag 079Q, remark-existence-D (ringed-site example), and Tag 07D9, lemma-derived-products (1)-(2)

proof.text:
For each distinguished triangle choose a cone-triangle representative $Q(K_i\xrightarrow{f_i}L_i\to C(f_i)\to K_i[1])$, using precisely the characterization in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. At degree $r$ the rebracketing of coproducts gives
$$\bigoplus_i C(f_i)^r=\bigoplus_i(L_i^r\oplus K_i^{r+1})\cong(\bigoplus_i L_i^r)\oplus(\bigoplus_i K_i^{r+1})=C(\bigoplus_i f_i)^r.$$
The differentials on both sides are the same block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\bigoplus d_{L_i}&\bigoplus f_i\\0&-\bigoplus d_{K_i}\end{pmatrix}$; the inclusion, the negative projection, and the shift are preserved by this identification. By the coproduct statement used in step 2 [lem-kun-grothendieck-derived-coproducts], the sum of the chosen triangles is therefore isomorphic to the cone triangle of $\bigoplus f_i$ in the derived category, hence distinguished. Coproducts of the originally chosen triangle isomorphisms are isomorphisms (sum their inverses). Closure of distinguished triangles under isomorphism proves the rest of (1). This calculation also covers the empty family, yielding the zero cone triangle.

source.place: (1), termwise sum of mapping-cone triangles; cone formula as in Stacks Tag 05RU/05RT

proof.text: Define the object predicate $P(K)$ by: $K$ belongs to every full replete triangulated subcategory closed under small sums and containing $\mathcal S$. The ambient derived category is one such subcategory. Every member of $\mathcal S$, and the zero object, satisfy $P$. If $P(K)$ holds then $P(K[n])$ holds for every $n\in\mathbf Z$, and the same is true after an isomorphism. If two vertices of a distinguished triangle satisfy $P$, they belong to every subcategory in the definition, so its third vertex also belongs to each of them. Likewise, a small family of objects satisfying $P$ has its ambient coproduct in every such subcategory, using (1). Thus the full subcategory on $P$ has all the required closure properties. It is contained in each of the subcategories defining it, which is exactly minimality. This proves (2). This is a pointwise intersection of object predicates in the ambient universe, not a colimit indexed by a proper class; no smallness of $\mathcal S$ is assumed.

Suppose $K\cong A\oplus B$ belongs to $\Loc(\mathcal S)$. Set $T=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbf N}(A\oplus B)$, which belongs to $\Loc(\mathcal S)$ by (1)-(2). There is an isomorphism $A\oplus T\cong T$: send the extra $A$ to the $A$-summand of copy $0$, send the $A$-summand of copy $n$ to the $A$-summand of copy $n+1$, and send the $B$-summand of copy $n$ to the $B$-summand of copy $n$. The inverse sends $A_0$ to the extra $A$, $A_{n+1}$ to $A_n$, and $B_n$ to $B_n$; both composites are identities on every coprojection. Hence $T\oplus A$ belongs to $\Loc(\mathcal S)$. The split triangle $T\xrightarrow{\mathrm{inl}}T\oplus A\xrightarrow{\mathrm{pr}_2}A\xrightarrow{0}T[1]$ is distinguished by [lem-sbc-biproduct-triangle-distinguished]. Its first two vertices lie in $\Loc(\mathcal S)$, so (2) puts $A$ there. Interchange $A,B$ for the other summand. Thus the localizing closure is thick by the definition [pur9-def-thick].

source.place: (3), Eilenberg swindle; split triangle is Stacks Tag 05QT, lemma-split (3)

proof.text: If $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal S'\subseteq\Loc(\mathcal S)$, the localizing category $\Loc(\mathcal S')$ contains $\mathcal S$, so minimality from (2) gives $\Loc(\mathcal S)\subseteq\Loc(\mathcal S')$. Conversely $\Loc(\mathcal S)$ is localizing and contains $\mathcal S'$, so the same minimality gives the opposite inclusion. This proves the last assertion of (3).
